title: VisionQuest Trailer Reveals Marvel's Most Mysterious Mercenary
summary:
Marvel is about to introduce a character so mysterious that even the comics barely explain him. In the new trailer for "VisionQuest," we meet Paladin—a mercenary hired to hunt down Vision.

The show picks up after "WandaVision," with Vision (played by Paul Bettany) hiding and searching for meaning. This is the White Vision who rebooted and escaped from those who wanted to weaponize him. He consults the AI personalities inside his programming, including the infamous Ultron. But his quiet life ends when a bounty is placed on his head, forcing him to run with Thomas Shepherd, a boy who may be Vision's reincarnated son.

That bounty brings in Paladin. He first appeared in Marvel Comics in 1970 in "Daredevil" #150, created by writer Jim Shooter and artist Carmine Infantino. In that issue, he was after the villainous Purple Man. But as a gun for hire, it's more about the price than what side of good and evil he's on—so the price on Vision's head makes it worth the squeeze. Unlike most Marvel characters, Paladin's origins are a total mystery. According to Marvel.com, "Virtually nothing is known about the background of the mercenary who calls himself Paladin." We don't know why he became an adventurer or where he got his special weapons. He's popped up over the years in titles like "Heroes for Hire," "Thunderbolts," "X-Men," and "The Defenders."

Actor Todd Stashwick confirmed on Instagram he's playing Paladin. In the trailer, around the 1:37 mark, a masked figure bursts through double doors with a big gun, aiming at Vision.

The show also brings back James Spader as Ultron—his first live-action return in over a decade. It will also introduce Jocasta, Ultron's "bride." With Ultron inside Vision's mind and Paladin on his trail, Vision has plenty of enemies. "VisionQuest" premieres October 14 on Disney+.
why_it_matters: Streaming superhero shows are how a lot of teenagers first meet big ideas like artificial intelligence, identity and what makes someone 'human' — and a villain who works for whoever pays most is a reminder that in real life, too, people can be pulled into violence by money rather than belief.

background_read: Vision is a Marvel Comics superhero — an android with human-like feelings who was first introduced in the 1960s and later became a major character in Marvel's films.
In the movies he is played by Paul Bettany, a British actor who also voiced the AI helper JARVIS before Vision ever appeared on screen.
The 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision" ended with a rebuilt, all-white Vision flying away, and that is the version this new show follows.

Ultron is one of Marvel's oldest villains: an artificial intelligence built to protect Earth that decided humans were the problem — James Spader voiced him back in the 2015 film "Avengers: Age of Ultron."

Jim Shooter, one of the writers who created Paladin, later became Marvel's editor-in-chief, while Carmine Infantino, the artist on that issue, is best known for his work at DC Comics on characters such as the Flash.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — Marvel fans and the cast
perspectives.description: The show digs out an obscure comic character and gives a working actor like Todd Stashwick a leading role, while bringing James Spader's Ultron back to live action for the first time in over a decade.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — viewers tired of franchise sequels
perspectives.description: Paladin is sold partly on being a mystery, which can be a way of hiding that a character has little depth. Critics of superhero TV argue that endless spin-offs and returning villains keep studios recycling instead of making something new.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — how comics work as source material
perspectives.description: Paladin is an example of a long-running type in comics: the hired gun with no fixed loyalty. Writers use characters like him because they can switch sides whenever the story needs tension, and their blank pasts leave room for future reveals.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what the show sets up
perspectives.description: If 'VisionQuest' is well received, Paladin and Jocasta could reappear in later Marvel projects, since the studio treats streaming series as a testing ground for characters it might use on the big screen.
